titel: Money market and cash in the US
kurz: Short-term investments do not build wealth; they keep money available, and this availability has a price that you should know.

bloecke.md:
## The money market and the federal funds rate

The [[Money market|money market]] is the market for loans with a term of up to one year, usually less than a week and often just a single night. Trading takes place between banks, the Federal Reserve, the Treasury, money market funds and large companies, in amounts that are out of the question for private investors. Nevertheless, this market determines how much interest arrives in your savings account at the end of the month.

The Federal Reserve steers it through a target range for the **federal funds rate**, the rate at which banks lend reserves to each other overnight without collateral. The range is 25 basis points wide and is set at the eight regular meetings of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) each year. The Fed holds the market rate in this range mainly through two administered rates: the interest it pays banks on their reserve balances and the rate of its overnight reverse repo facility, which money market funds can also use. No bank lends money overnight at a lower rate than it receives from the Fed, and no money market fund invests below the rate it can get at the Fed.

The New York Fed publishes two reference rates every business day, calculated from transactions actually settled: the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) and the **Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR)**, the rate for overnight loans secured by Treasury securities. SOFR replaced the survey-based dollar Libor, which was discontinued in June 2023. Every change in the target range moves these rates, money market fund yields and Treasury bill yields within days. Interest rates on savings accounts follow with a delay of weeks and rarely in full.

## Four ways to invest short-term money

Private investors have four ways of investing money in this market. They differ less in the interest rate than in legal form, availability, protection and tax.

With a **high-yield savings account** or a money market deposit account, the money is held as a deposit at a bank. It is available every day and earns a variable rate. The rate only applies until further notice, because the bank may change it at any time.

With a **certificate of deposit (CD)**, the money is invested for a fixed term, and the interest rate is locked in for that time. Early withdrawal usually costs a penalty of several months of interest. Brokered CDs bought through a brokerage account usually cannot be redeemed early at all; they can only be sold on the secondary market at the current price. If interest rates rise, you remain tied to the old rate; if they fall, that rate is secured. The fixed rate works in both directions.

The third option is **money market funds**. Under SEC Rule 2a-7, they may only hold short-term, high-quality debt. Government money market funds invest almost entirely in Treasury bills, other government securities and repurchase agreements backed by them. Government and retail funds aim for a stable share price of $1.00, while institutional prime funds have a floating price. The units are securities, not deposits. If the fund company goes bust, the fund's assets remain separate. In return, there is no deposit insurance and no promised interest rate, and the sponsor has no obligation to support the fund.

The fourth option is **Treasury bills**. The US Treasury issues them with terms of 4, 6, 8, 13, 17, 26 and 52 weeks, at a discount and without a coupon, through regular auctions. You can buy them at auction through TreasuryDirect or through a broker, which also offers older bills on the secondary market. If you hold a bill until maturity, the result is already fixed on the day you buy it; if you sell earlier, you bear the price risk. Interest on Treasury securities is exempt from state and local income tax.

bloecke.md:
Money market funds show how closely cash depends on monetary policy. Their yield is usually quoted as the seven-day SEC yield, after fund expenses. From the end of 2008 to the end of 2015 and again from March 2020 to March 2022, the Fed held its target range at 0% to 0.25%. In those years, many money market funds yielded almost nothing, and sponsors waived part of their fees to avoid negative returns. A money market fund therefore offers no guarantee and delivers the market's short-term rate, whether interest rates are rising or falling.

In September 2008, after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, whose short-term debt it held, the Reserve Primary Fund "broke the buck": its share price fell to $0.97. Investors withdrew money from other prime funds en masse, and the Treasury temporarily guaranteed money market fund shares. The SEC has since tightened the rules several times, in 2010, 2014 and 2023. Government money market funds, which hold almost only government debt, were and are the more conservative type.

A high-yield savings account and a Treasury bill are both assumed to yield 4.00%. Both bring in $400 of interest in one year. There is no withholding and no allowance to assign: the bank sends Form 1099-INT if the interest reaches $10, and the interest is taxed as ordinary income.

In the 22% federal bracket and with a state income tax of 5%, $88 of federal tax and $20 of state tax are due on the savings interest, leaving $292. On the Treasury bill, only the federal tax applies, leaving $312. For a bill bought at a discount, the interest is taxed in the year it matures, which can shift the tax into the next year.

In states without an income tax, the difference disappears; in states with high rates, it is larger. Government money market funds pass on the state tax advantage only for the part of their income that comes from Treasury securities, and some states require a minimum share for this. For the decision, availability, protection and state tax therefore matter more than the last tenth of a percentage point.

## Scope and limits of deposit insurance

The FDIC insures deposits at member banks up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category; the National Credit Union Administration provides the same coverage for credit unions. Ownership categories include single accounts, joint accounts, certain retirement accounts such as IRAs, and trust accounts. A joint account with two owners is therefore covered up to $500,000. Since April 2024, trust accounts are covered at $250,000 per beneficiary, for up to five beneficiaries per owner. When a bank fails, the FDIC usually pays out insured deposits within a few business days, often by transferring them to another bank.

The following restrictions apply to this protection:

- The limit applies to all of a depositor's accounts in the same ownership category at one bank combined. Several accounts at the same bank therefore share one limit, and different brand names of the same bank count as one bank.
- Only deposits are insured. Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, money market funds, annuities and crypto assets are not, even if they were bought at a bank branch.
- Deposit networks and brokerage sweep programs spread larger amounts across several banks so that each portion stays within the limit. Money you hold directly at one of these banks counts toward the same limit there.
- With fintech apps that hold customer money at partner banks, deposit insurance only passes through to you if the records of who owns which deposit are correct. The bankruptcy of the intermediary Synapse in 2024 showed that this is not guaranteed.

bloecke.md:
On 10 March 2023, California regulators closed Silicon Valley Bank, and the FDIC took over as receiver. The day before, customers had tried to withdraw tens of billions of dollars, most of them companies whose deposits far exceeded the insured limit. On 12 March, after Signature Bank had also been closed, the Treasury, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC decided to protect all depositors of both banks, including uninsured ones, using the systemic risk exception.

This rescue of uninsured deposits was an exceptional decision, not a legal entitlement. In earlier failures, such as IndyMac in 2008, depositors above the limit initially received only part of their uninsured balance. Deposit insurance therefore protects up to the limit; anything above it depends on the bank's remaining assets or on decisions taken in a crisis.

bloecke.unter: The limit has been raised step by step since 1934; since 2010, the $250,000 limit has been permanent and has not been changed since.

bloecke.md:
Banks advertise promotional rates for new customers and cash bonuses for opening an account or setting up direct deposit. Promotional rates often apply only for a few months and only to new money up to a maximum amount. After that, the rate falls to the standard rate, which can change at any time. Bonuses are taxable income.

Illustrative calculation for $20,000 over twelve months: 4.25% in the first half-year brings in $425. If the rate then falls to an assumed 1.75%, a further $175 is added, $600 in total or an effective 3.0%. A permanent offer at 2.60% brings in $520. The advantage is $80 gross and $62.40 after federal tax in the 22% bracket. This requires opening another account and a date in the calendar on which the money has to be moved. A comparison that leaves out the fallback phase overstates the advantage of the teaser offer.

bloecke.md:
## Benefits and costs of cash

Howard Marks describes liquidity as patient opportunism. Investors who hold cash can act when an opportunity arises without having to sell something first. The value of this option rises when prices fall, that is, in phases when other investors are forced to sell. It is paid for with the return forgone compared with long-term investments. Cash itself often loses purchasing power after tax and inflation, in the waterfall above about 0.3% a year, so around $270 on $100,000, and considerably more in years with high inflation or near-zero interest rates.

Over long periods, cash performs considerably worse than equities. Dimson, Marsh and Staunton measure a real return of 0.5% a year for the US money market from 1900 to 2025. One dollar grew to $69 in nominal terms and $1.80 in real terms, a gain in purchasing power of 80% in 126 years. Invested in equities, the dollar grew to 3,296 times its value in real terms. Since 1928, the US equity premium over the money market has been 6.65 percentage points a year.

For money that stays invested for a long time, cash is therefore the worst investment, and for money that will be needed soon, the only sensible one. Moreover, the option to buy when prices fall only has value if it is used. Investors who have been waiting for years for the right moment to get in bear the costs year after year without ever benefiting.

The interest on cash compensates for the loss of purchasing power, usually not in full, and is thus not a return. Whether money should be held as cash therefore depends on whether its purpose requires safety; the level of interest plays no role in this.

- Match the term to the purpose. An [[Emergency fund|emergency fund]] belongs in a high-yield savings account or a government money market fund, money for a known expense in a year in a Treasury bill or a CD with a matching term.
- Check what your "cash" at a broker actually is: a bank sweep deposit, a money market fund or a credit balance at the broker. Interest rate and protection differ.
- Spread amounts over $250,000 across several banks or ownership categories, and use the FDIC's BankFind tool to check whether two brands belong to the same bank.
- In states with high income tax, compare savings rates after state tax with Treasury bills or Treasury-only money market funds.
- Note promotional rates with their end date and include the fallback rate in the comparison.

Savings accounts, CDs, money market funds and Treasury bills differ above all in legal form, protection and tax; only savings accounts and CDs are deposits with FDIC insurance.
FDIC insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category; joint, retirement and trust accounts add separate coverage, and investments bought at a bank are not covered.
Interest on Treasury bills is exempt from state and local income tax, which can make them the better choice in high-tax states at the same rate.
After federal tax and inflation, cash usually earns a real return close to zero or below; this loss of purchasing power is the price of availability.
